questions.q: Why does an untagged GPU resource create a bigger blind spot in cost reporting than an untagged CPU resource?
options: Untagged GPU resources are automatically shut down by the cloud provider, so this is not actually a real problem
GPU resources cannot be tagged at all in either Azure or AWS
Tagging only applies to storage resources, never to compute
The GPU resource accumulates spend in the same uncounted 'Untagged' bucket, but at a much higher per-hour rate, so the same blind spot hides far more money per hour it goes unnoticed
questions.explain: The tagging mechanism is identical to standard compute, but because GPU spend has a much higher per-hour rate, the same untagged blind spot conceals a far larger dollar amount for every hour it persists.

questions.q: Why does the lesson recommend a `job-type` tag (e.g., training vs. inference) specifically for AI infrastructure?
options: Because training and inference always cost the exact same amount, so the tag is purely cosmetic
Because cloud providers require this exact tag name on every resource by law

Training and inference have very different right-sizing profiles, so separating them in cost reports lets a team tell whether a cost increase came from a bigger training run or from growing inference traffic
Because without it, GPU instances cannot be billed at all
questions.explain: Since training and inference differ so much in memory/compute needs, a job-type tag lets cost reports distinguish which side of that split drove a spend increase, rather than collapsing both into one undifferentiated GPU number.

questions.q: Why does the lesson recommend tighter, GPU-specific budget thresholds rather than relying on one subscription-wide budget?
options: A subscription-wide budget set at 80%/100% can take days to trip on GPU overspend because it's diluted inside the whole bill, while a budget scoped to GPU-tagged spend catches the same overspend far earlier
Subscription-wide budgets are not supported by any major cloud provider
GPU-specific budgets are required by default and cannot be disabled
Tighter thresholds on GPU spend have no actual effect on how quickly an alert fires
questions.explain: Because GPU spend has much higher cost velocity, a dedicated, narrower budget scoped to GPU-tagged resources with tighter thresholds notices a spike far sooner than a general subscription-wide budget would.

questions.q: What advantage does a forecasted-spend budget threshold offer over an actual-spend threshold for GPU budgets?
options: It eliminates the need for tagging entirely
It can fire an alert based on projected month-end spend, catching a runaway GPU cost trend before the month even ends, rather than after actual spend crosses the line
It guarantees the cloud provider will automatically stop all GPU instances
It only applies to CPU resources, never to GPU resources
questions.explain: A forecasted threshold projects where spend is trending and can alert before the month closes, which matters more for GPU workloads given how fast their spend can accumulate.

questions.q: According to the lesson, what does a complete FinOps practice for AI infrastructure actually combine?
options: Only a single company-wide spending cap with no further detail

Tagging every training job, disciplined training-vs-inference right-sizing, spot GPUs paired with checkpointing, and dedicated GPU-specific budgets and anomaly detection, working together as one ongoing loop
A one-time audit performed only at the end of each fiscal year
Switching every GPU workload to on-demand pricing and avoiding spot entirely
questions.explain: The chapter frames tagging, right-sizing, spot/checkpointing, and GPU-specific budgets/anomaly detection as one combined, ongoing practice - not isolated tips - because of how much faster GPU spend moves than general cloud spend.
